strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer vision problem: reconstructing sharp, animatable human avatars from motion-blurred multiview videos. Combining exposure-integrated Gaussian rendering with articulated sub-frame motion optimization is a coherent contribution, even though its constituent techniques build on existing work.

The improvements are substantial and consistent across synthetic and real data. Relative to GauHuman, PSNR increases from 23.080 to 25.546 dB on synthetic data and from 25.602 to 27.010 dB on real data; LPIPS improves from 0.2277 to 0.1476 and from 0.2380 to 0.1668, respectively. Figures 4–5 also show clearer limbs and clothing details.

The real capture benchmark strengthens the empirical contribution beyond synthetic averaging. Four long-exposure training cameras and eight synchronized short-exposure evaluation cameras provide a practical test of sharp novel-view reconstruction across eight scenes.

The ablations support the principal design choices. Removing pose interpolation reduces PSNR by 1.537 dB on synthetic data and 1.185 dB on real data. Table 6 specifically tests temporal ambiguity: inter-frame regularization improves non-middle-timestep PSNR by approximately 1.0–1.4 dB across blur magnitudes, while largely preserving midpoint quality.

Overall, the demonstrated reconstruction improvements, real capture evaluation, and targeted motion ablations provide a stronger case for acceptance than rejection. The reservations primarily concern reproducibility, comparison scope, and the extent of the motion-recovery claims.
weaknesses: The comparisons establish superiority over GauHuman and four deblurring-plus-GauHuman pipelines, but leave important attribution questions unresolved. The manuscript does not specify deblurrer checkpoints or adaptation, whether SMPL initialization is recomputed after deblurring, or whether optimization budgets are matched. The explanation that multiview inconsistency causes the two-stage methods' weak performance is plausible but not directly measured. Related dynamic deblurring methods cited in Section 2 are not experimentally assessed or discussed as potential adapted baselines.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The supplied manuscript does not specify the architectures of the pose-displacement and skinning-offset networks, control-pose initialization, training duration, or learning rates for the newly introduced parameters. It also leaves root translation handling and skinning-weight normalization unclear. Training time and memory usage are absent despite rendering several virtual frames per observation, and no code or dataset URL accompanies the availability claim.

The temporal prior has a physical mismatch that deserves analysis. Equation 15 penalizes differences between consecutive exposure endpoints, although the real capture uses 50 ms exposures at 15 FPS, leaving roughly 16.7 ms of unobserved motion between exposures. It also regularizes the spline poses before the learned displacement correction. Thus, the prior encourages continuity heuristically rather than explicitly modeling the full trajectory and capture timing.

The evidence supports sharp novel-view reconstruction more strongly than accurate motion recovery or general animation. There are no direct pose-accuracy measurements or quantitative evaluations on unseen driving poses. Non-middle-timestep evaluation is restricted to synthetic data, and the dependence on estimated foreground masks produces acknowledged foreground/background blending failures. These limitations narrow the demonstrated applicability.

Several correctable formulation and reporting issues reduce clarity. Equation 12 appears to omit the standard B-spline normalization factor 1/(P−1)!, and the treatment of rotation vectors versus interpolation on SO(3) is not explained. Table 8 reports values matching the unregularized rows of Table 6 rather than the full model in Table 9. The claim of substantial midpoint gains from regularization overstates Table 6, while shape optimization contributes negligible gains. Section 2.1 also contains duplicated text.

Figures 4–5 show corresponding improvements in limb boundaries and clothing details.

The benchmark construction is valuable. Six synthetic subjects and eight real scenes provide complementary evidence, and the synchronized hybrid-exposure system enables evaluation against sharp images from held-out viewpoints. Overall, the supported reconstruction gains, real-capture validation, and useful benchmark favor weak acceptance. The reservations below limit reproducibility and the breadth of the claims, but do not outweigh the demonstrated contribution.
weaknesses: Comparative evidence is concentrated on GauHuman and four deblur-then-GauHuman pipelines. Their nearly identical PSNR results warrant more analysis: the manuscript does not specify deblurring checkpoint/adaptation details or clearly establish whether poses are re-estimated after deblurring. Consequently, attributing their failure specifically to multiview inconsistency is not established. Related dynamic-scene deblurring methods are discussed but not experimentally assessed.

Important implementation details are missing from the supplied manuscript, including motion-network architectures, control-point initialization, training duration, and specific optimization settings for the added motion parameters. Referring to original 3DGS learning rates does not fully specify these new components. Training time and memory are also unreported despite requiring multiple renders per observation.

The mathematical specification needs correction or clarification. Equation 12 appears to omit the standard B-spline normalization factor 1/(P−1)!, so it does not preserve constant control poses as written. Rotation-vector interpolation is described as operating in SO(3) without explaining representation discontinuities. Equation 15 regularizes the spline poses before the learned displacement, rather than the final poses; thus its stated continuity interpretation is incomplete. These issues do not prove the implementation is incorrect, but prevent faithful reproduction.

The demonstrated scope is narrower than unrestricted sharp, animatable avatar recovery. Evaluation emphasizes held-out views of captured motions, without a clear quantitative test on unseen driving poses or direct 3D motion accuracy. Non-middle-timestep validation is synthetic only. The acknowledged foreground/background blending problem and reliance on precomputed masks further constrain practical use.

Several smaller reporting issues reduce clarity: Section 2.1 repeats substantial text; real-image resolution differs between Table 1 and the prose; and Table 8 uses values matching the unregularized rows of Table 6 without identifying this configuration. Claims that shape optimization is important are also stronger than its tiny or occasionally negative measured gains. These are secondary concerns rather than independent grounds for rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: reconstructing sharp, animatable human avatars from motion-blurred multi-view videos. Combining an articulated Gaussian avatar with exposure integration and joint sub-frame pose optimization is a useful, coherent contribution, even though its individual ingredients build on established methods.

The quantitative improvements are substantial and consistent across metrics. On synthetic data, PSNR increases from 23.089 for the strongest reported baseline to 25.546, while LPIPS decreases from 0.2205 to 0.1476. On real data, PSNR improves from 25.602 to 27.010 and LPIPS from 0.2342 to 0.1668. Figures 4–5 also show clearer moving limbs and clothing details.

The evaluation includes six synthetic subjects and eight real scenes. The synchronized hybrid-exposure capture system, with four blurry training views and eight sharp evaluation views, provides particularly valuable evidence beyond simulated blur. Held-out camera evaluation and foreground bounding-box metrics strengthen the experimental design.

The ablations substantiate the main motion-model choices. Removing pose interpolation reduces PSNR by 1.537 dB on synthetic data and 1.185 dB on real data. Table 6 directly tests temporal ordering: inter-frame regularization improves non-middle-timestep PSNR by approximately 1.0–1.4 dB across blur magnitudes. These results make the supported contribution stronger than the remaining reservations and favor weak acceptance.
weaknesses: The comparisons establish improvement over GauHuman and four deblurring-plus-GauHuman pipelines, but do not fully isolate the benefit over simpler blur-aware articulated reconstruction. Table 7 shows that two control points perform almost identically to four, suggesting that much of the gain may come from joint exposure modeling rather than the particular spline design. Dynamic-scene deblurring methods discussed in related work are not evaluated. The contribution is therefore better supported as a useful integration than as a broadly superior motion-modeling advance.

Important reproducibility details are missing from the supplied manuscript: network architectures, initialization of sub-frame control parameters, training iterations, learning rates for newly introduced parameters, and baseline checkpoint or fine-tuning settings. Training time and memory costs are also absent despite requiring multiple renders per observation. The text asserts public code and data availability but provides no accessible pointer in the manuscript.

The mathematical specification needs correction or clarification. Equation 12 appears to omit the standard B-spline normalization factor 1/(P−1)!, so the stated basis does not form a partition of unity. Equations 11 and 14 interpolate and add three-dimensional rotation parameters without explaining their representation or handling of rotation discontinuities. These issues do not establish that the implementation is incorrect, but prevent faithful reproduction of the stated motion model.

The temporal prior has an unexamined modeling limitation. Equation 15 encourages adjacent exposure endpoints to coincide, although the real capture uses 50 ms exposures at 15 FPS, leaving an approximately 16.7 ms gap. It also regularizes the spline poses rather than the final residual-corrected poses. Table 6 supports its empirical usefulness on synthetic data, but does not validate accurate physical trajectories under these real capture conditions.

Evidence for motion recovery and animation is narrower than evidence for novel-view reconstruction. There is no quantitative pose or trajectory evaluation, real non-middle-timestep ground truth is unavailable, and no explicit unseen-pose animation evaluation is reported. Furthermore, the acknowledged dependence on hard foreground masks excludes correct foreground-background mixing at moving boundaries, limiting the physical accuracy and applicability of the blur model.

Several reporting issues are correctable rather than rejection-level flaws: Section 2.1 repeats substantial text; the real image resolution differs between Table 1 and the prose; and Table 8's proposed-method results match the unregularized rows of Table 6 rather than the full-model results in Table 9. Claims of substantial middle-timestep improvements from regularization also overstate the small, occasionally negative changes in Table 6.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: reconstructing sharp, animatable human avatars directly from motion-blurred videos. Combining exposure-integrated Gaussian rendering with an articulated motion prior is a coherent contribution beyond independently deblurring input views.

The central empirical result is convincing across synthetic and real data. Table 2 improves over GauHuman from 23.080 to 25.546 dB on synthetic data and from 25.602 to 27.010 dB on real captures, with substantial SSIM and LPIPS improvements. Figures 4 and 6 also show clearer contours and clothing details.

The synchronized real benchmark is a valuable contribution: four long-exposure training cameras and eight short-exposure evaluation cameras provide held-out sharp views across eight scenes. Exposure synchronization and neutral-density filtering make this stronger evidence than synthetic blur alone.

The ablations meaningfully support the motion modeling. Removing pose interpolation substantially reduces reconstruction quality, while Table 4 specifically demonstrates that temporal regularization improves non-midpoint rendering by approximately 1.0–1.4 dB across blur levels. Tests of view count, initialization perturbations, masks, and blur magnitude provide useful robustness evidence.

The demonstrated reconstruction gains and real-data benchmark outweigh the reservations below, supporting weak acceptance. The qualitative AMASS animation results also establish potential usefulness beyond reproducing observed poses.
weaknesses: Comparative positioning is incomplete. All quantitative competitors use GauHuman, with or without 2D restoration; the cited dynamic-scene deblurring approaches are discussed only briefly. These experiments establish an advantage over practical two-stage pipelines, but less clearly isolate the advance over existing joint 3D reconstruction and deblurring methods. The attribution of two-stage failures specifically to cross-view inconsistency is plausible but not directly measured.

Important implementation details are missing: the pose and skinning network architectures, initialization of distinct motion control points, training duration, sequence lengths and temporal sampling, and learning rates for newly introduced parameters. Referring to original 3DGS schedules does not fully specify the new optimization. Training time and memory are also unreported despite rendering multiple samples per exposure.

The mathematical description needs correction or clarification. Equation 6 appears to omit the standard 1/(P−1)! normalization of the uniform B-spline matrix. Rotations are interpolated and added as three-vectors without clearly explaining their conversion to SO(3) or the geodesic calculation. Equation 9 regularizes the pre-displacement poses rather than the final corrected poses, leaving the connection to final-motion continuity insufficiently explained. These are formulation and reproducibility concerns, rather than evidence that the reported results are invalid.

Some component-level claims exceed the evidence. Table 5 shows negligible differences between B-splines and simpler interpolation, and shape optimization has very small or occasionally negative effects in Tables 11 and 14. Without variability estimates, claims of B-spline superiority and the necessity of every component are too strong.

The physical and generalization claims need qualification. As acknowledged, averaging sRGB values is not physically accurate exposure integration, and SMPL cannot explain independently moving accessories or loose garments. Real-data evaluation covers only exposure midpoints; sub-frame motion accuracy is supported by synthetic rendering metrics rather than direct motion measurements. Novel-pose animation and monocular smartphone generalization remain qualitative demonstrations.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: reconstructing sharp, animatable human avatars directly from motion-blurred videos. Combining exposure-integrated rendering with articulated motion optimization is a coherent contribution, even though its individual ingredients build on established methods.

The main improvements are substantial and supported by both synthetic and real data. Table 2 reports 25.546 versus 23.080 dB for GauHuman on synthetic data, and 27.010 versus 25.602 dB on real data, alongside considerable LPIPS improvements. Figures 4 and 6 show corresponding improvements in contours and texture.

The real capture benchmark is a valuable experimental contribution: four long-exposure training cameras and eight synchronized short-exposure evaluation cameras provide held-out sharp viewpoints across eight scenes. This complements the six-subject synthetic evaluation and reduces dependence on simulated blur.

The ablations support the principal mechanisms. Removing pose interpolation substantially reduces reconstruction quality, while Table 4 shows that temporal regularization improves non-middle-timestep PSNR by approximately 1.0–1.4 dB across blur levels, directly supporting its intended role in resolving temporal ambiguity.

Evaluation covers several blur magnitudes, training-view counts, initialization perturbations, mask sources, and temporal sampling choices. Taken together, the practical contribution and consistent empirical gains support weak acceptance despite the technical and reproducibility reservations below.
weaknesses: Comparative evidence is restricted to GauHuman and four deblur-then-GauHuman pipelines. The paper cites related dynamic-scene deblurring methods, including DyBluRF and BARD-GS, but does not empirically distinguish its reconstruction quality from these approaches where comparison is feasible. They need not support animatable avatars to provide relevant rendering comparisons. The claimed explanation that two-stage methods fail specifically because of multiview inconsistency is also not isolated experimentally.

The motion equations contain consequential specification ambiguities. Equation 6 appears to omit the standard 1/(P−1)! normalization of the uniform B-spline matrix; for P=4, the resulting basis weights sum to six rather than one. Equations 5 and 8 operate on rotation coordinates without explaining rotation wrapping or manifold treatment. Equation 9 regularizes the pre-displacement poses rather than the final poses used for rendering. These issues do not establish that the implementation fails, but prevent confident reproduction of the stated motion model.

Implementation details are insufficient for independent reproduction. The pose-displacement and LBS networks are described only as CNNs, without architectures; training iterations, sequence lengths, control-point initialization, and treatment of global translation are unspecified. Referring to the original 3DGS learning-rate schedule does not specify optimization of the additional motion parameters. Training time and memory are also absent despite rendering multiple samples per exposure.

Some component claims exceed the evidence. In Table 5, B-splines improve synthetic PSNR over linear interpolation by only 0.030 dB, and SLERP slightly exceeds their real-data PSNR. Shape optimization has negligible or occasionally negative effects in Tables 11 and 14. Without variability estimates, these results support the overall framework more strongly than the claimed necessity or superiority of every component.

Accurate motion recovery and broad generalization are less established than sharp novel-view rendering. There are no quantitative pose or trajectory errors; real-data temporal evaluation is limited to exposure midpoints; novel-pose animation and smartphone reconstruction are qualitative demonstrations. The acknowledged inability to model loose garments and handheld objects further limits the applicable motion class.

The physical formulation is approximate: the method averages nonlinear sRGB values, a limitation acknowledged in Section 4.5.2. Separately, Equation 1 omits the exposure normalization needed to match Equation 2. The latter is a correctable presentation issue, whereas the former limits claims of physically accurate blur formation.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: reconstructing sharp, animatable human avatars from motion-blurred videos. Combining exposure-integrated Gaussian rendering with articulated motion optimization provides a coherent solution, although its individual ingredients build on established techniques.

The main improvements are substantial and supported by real captures. In Table 2, the method improves over GauHuman from 23.080 to 25.546 dB on synthetic data and from 25.602 to 27.010 dB on real data, with corresponding SSIM and LPIPS improvements. Figures 4 and 6 show visibly sharper contours and clothing details.

The real benchmark is a valuable contribution: four long-exposure training cameras and eight synchronized short-exposure evaluation cameras provide held-out sharp views across eight scenes. Exposure synchronization and neutral-density filtering make the evaluation more convincing than synthetic blur alone.

The ablations meaningfully support the motion-model design. Removing pose interpolation substantially degrades reconstruction, while inter-frame regularization improves non-middle-timestep PSNR by approximately 1.0–1.4 dB across blur levels (Table 4), directly supporting its intended role in resolving temporal ambiguity.

Experiments cover different blur magnitudes, training-view counts, initialization perturbations, and segmentation methods. Together with qualitative novel-pose animation, this evidence makes the case for acceptance stronger than the remaining reservations.
weaknesses: Comparisons use only GauHuman as the avatar backbone, optionally preceded by four video deblurring methods. Cited dynamic-scene deblurring approaches such as BARD-GS and DyBluRF are not evaluated, even for the overlapping novel-view reconstruction task. The results establish superiority over the tested pipelines, but less clearly isolate the advantage over existing joint 3D deblurring strategies. The claim that cross-view inconsistency explains the two-stage methods' failure is plausible but not directly measured.

The mathematical specification needs correction and clarification. Equation 6 appears to omit the standard 1/(P−1)! B-spline normalization; for P=4, the stated basis weights sum to six rather than one. Rotation interpolation and additive corrections are expressed in three-vector coordinates without explaining their relationship to SO(3), and Equation 9 regularizes the pre-correction poses rather than the final poses. These issues hinder faithful implementation, although they do not by themselves invalidate the empirical results.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the pose-displacement and LBS networks lack architectural details, and training iterations, sequence lengths, control-point initialization, and handling of global translation are insufficiently specified. Training time and memory costs are also absent despite rendering multiple subframes per observation. A promised code release does not resolve these omissions in the submitted manuscript.

Some component-level claims exceed the evidence. B-splines perform almost identically to linear interpolation and SLERP in Table 5, while shape optimization contributes little and sometimes reduces PSNR or SSIM (Tables 11 and 14). Without variability estimates, these results support continuous motion parameterization more strongly than the necessity of the particular spline or every refinement component.

The broader motion-recovery and generalization claims remain less established than novel-view image quality. Real-data evaluation measures only exposure midpoints; pose accuracy is assessed visually rather than quantitatively. Novel-pose animation and smartphone reconstruction are qualitative demonstrations. The acknowledged use of sRGB averaging and inability to model independently moving garments or accessories further limit the physical fidelity and scope of the method.
